title: La Vita Inimitabile: from Pescara to the Vittoriale
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Pescara, the birth house on Corso Manthonè
stops.campa: In the house of Francesco Paolo Rapagnetta-d'Annunzio, above the fish-smelling river port of Pescara, a son is born on 12 March 1863. The Adriatic light comes in off the water and fills the room. The father, half-drunk on pride, will spend a fortune making a prince of him. The midwives say the child does not cry. The name itself is an annunciation: d'Annunzio, of the Announcement; the family hears the angel in it, and so will Italy.
suggested_refs: Museo Casa Natale Gabriele d'Annunzio, Corso Manthonè 116

stops.name: The Adriatic off Pescara, the legend of the brigantine Irene
stops.campa: The other birth, the one the poet himself will tell: not in a bed but on the deck of the brigantine Irene, pitching in the March Adriatic, the newborn washed by spray before he is washed by any priest. Born on the sea, of the sea: the legend runs ahead of the man all his life, and he never contradicts it, because it is truer than the register of the parish. The wave that rocked the cradle will carry him to Buccari and to Fiume.
suggested_refs: 19th-century Adriatic brigantine imagery; the Irene legend in early biographies
sources: Lucy Hughes-Hallett, The Pike: Gabriele d'Annunzio (2013)

stops.name: Prato, the Cicognini college
stops.campa: Eleven years old, the boy is sent north to the Cicognini at Prato, the sternest college in Tuscany, so that the Abruzzo dialect may be burned out of him and pure Tuscan set in its place. He writes home that he intends to be first in everything, and he is: first in Latin, first in insubordination, first in the punishment cells. In the dormitory he reads Carducci by contraband candle. The masters record a prodigy; the prodigy records himself.
suggested_refs: Convitto Nazionale Cicognini, Piazza del Collegio, Prato
sources: John Woodhouse, Gabriele D'Annunzio: Defiant Archangel (Oxford, 1998)

stops.name: Chieti, Primo Vere printed at sixteen
stops.campa: Still a schoolboy in uniform, he gives the printer Ricci of Chieti a sheaf of verses in the metres of Carducci's Odi barbare. His father pays for the edition. Primo Vere, First Spring, goes out into Italy signed by a sixteen-year-old, and Giuseppe Chiarini reviews it in the Fanfulla della Domenica: a new poet exists. In the college at Prato the boy reads his own name in the national press and understands, once and for all, that fame is a substance that can be manufactured.
suggested_refs: First edition of Primo Vere (Chieti, Ricci, 1879)

stops.name: The road to Francavilla, the first death of the poet
stops.campa: On 13 November 1880 the Gazzetta della Domenica of Florence announces that Gabriele d'Annunzio, the young poet of whom it has often spoken, has died on the road to Francavilla, thrown from his horse. Italy mourns the boy Muse. The letter announcing the death was written by the poet himself, signed G. Rutini; days later he rises from the dead to publish the corrected second edition of Primo Vere. It is the first myth he authors of himself: he learns that his own death is his best material, and he will die twice more before the end.
suggested_refs: Gazzetta della Domenica, 13 November 1880; second edition of Primo Vere (Carabba, 1880)

stops.name: Prato, the licence with honour, the college left behind
stops.campa: In the summer of 1881 he takes his licenza with honour and walks out of the Cicognini gates for the last time, eighteen years old, already the author of two books and one resurrection. Elda Zucconi, his Tuscan first love, is left behind in the pages of Canto Novo taking the sea-name Lalla. The masters who caned him will boast of him for a century. He turns south for one last Abruzzo summer, then aims himself at Rome like a projectile.
suggested_refs: Cicognini registers; Canto Novo (1882)

stops.name: Rome, arrival at Termini, the university abandoned before it begins
stops.campa: In November 1881 the train from the Abruzzo sets him down in Umbertine Rome. He enrols in Letters at the Sapienza and never sits an examination: the city itself is the faculty. Byzantine Rome of the speculators and the salons takes the small, cat-eyed provincial and finds him already fluent in its language. Within weeks he is in the newspapers; within a year he is the most talked-of young man in the capital. The Tiber, he decides, is his second river after the Pescara.
suggested_refs: Umbertine Rome photographs, 1880s; Stazione Termini

stops.name: Via dell'Umiltà, Cronaca Bizantina and Canto Novo
stops.campa: Angelo Sommaruga's Cronaca Bizantina gathers the golden youth of literary Rome, and d'Annunzio becomes its ornament. In May 1882 Sommaruga publishes Canto Novo, verses salted with the Adriatic, sunburnt, pagan: Rome discovers that the boy poet has a body and is not ashamed of it. He writes society chronicle, he duels in print, he dresses beyond his means. The Bizantina crowd calls itself decadent as a boast; he alone means to make decadence into empire.
stops.quote: Bisogna fare la propria vita, come si fa un'opera d'arte.
stops.quote_source: Il Piacere (1889), the credo already lived in the Roman years
suggested_refs: Cronaca Bizantina mastheads, 1882-1885; Canto Novo first edition

stops.name: Florence, the elopement train with Maria Hardouin
stops.campa: At the end of June 1883 he boards the Florence train with Maria Hardouin di Gallese, the duke's daughter, twenty years old and already carrying his child. The scandal is arranged like a stanza: flight, pursuit, discovery in Florence, the ruined honour of a ducal house. Rome talks of nothing else, which is the point. The duke rages, the mother relents, and the poet, who has read every romance and written better ones, waits calmly for the wedding he has made inevitable.
suggested_refs: Portraits of Maria Hardouin di Gallese

stops.name: Rome, the marriage in the chapel of Palazzo Altemps
stops.campa: On 28 July 1883, in the private chapel of Palazzo Altemps, Gabriele d'Annunzio marries Maria Hardouin di Gallese. The duke does not attend. The groom is twenty, famous, and insolvent; the bride's family considers itself dishonoured by a poet and does not yet know that in fifty years the poet will be the only reason it is remembered. Mario, the first of three sons, is born in January. The marriage will dissolve into affairs and debts, but the title of duchess consort trails him like incense.
suggested_refs: Palazzo Altemps, chapel of Sant'Aniceto

stops.name: La Tribuna, Duca Minimo, chronicler of elegance
stops.campa: For the Tribuna he becomes Duca Minimo, the Smallest Duke, and invents modern celebrity journalism from inside: chronicles of concerts, funerals, jewellers' windows, women's shoulders at the Palazzo Farnese balls. He furnishes the Roman bourgeoisie with its dreams and prices. From these columns he quarries Il Piacere; every countess he describes is a study, every drawing-room a set. He earns much, spends triple, and learns the arithmetic of glamour: debt is merely fame that has not yet been paid for.
suggested_refs: La Tribuna columns signed Duca Minimo, 1884-1888

stops.name: Outside Porta del Popolo, the saber duel and the scar
stops.campa: Journalism in Byzantine Rome is settled with sabers. In the meadows beyond the walls the poet meets the journalist Carlo Magnico on the field of honour and takes a blade across the scalp. The wound is dressed with iron perchloride; the tradition holds that the treatment costs him his hair, and the famous gleaming skull of the Comandante is minted here, on a Roman duelling ground, at twenty-two. He fights other duels and loses none of them in the telling. The scar becomes part of the iconography.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the bald d'Annunzio; duelling culture of Umbertine Rome

stops.name: Francavilla al Mare, the Conventino of Michetti, Il Piacere written
stops.campa: In the summer of 1888 he shuts himself in the sea-facing convent that Francesco Paolo Michetti has made his studio at Francavilla. The cenacolo gathers: Michetti painting, Tosti at the piano, Barbella modelling clay, the poet writing in monastic fury. In six months of Adriatic light he composes Il Piacere, giving Rome its Andrea Sperelli: the aesthete as hero, the life made artwork. Treves publishes it in May 1889 and the novel fixes the type of the Italian decadent forever. The convent, he says, is his true university.
suggested_refs: Convento Michetti (MuMi), Francavilla al Mare; Michetti's portraits of d'Annunzio

stops.name: San Vito Chietino, the Eremo on the Trabocchi coast, with Barbara Leoni
stops.campa: Summer 1889: with Barbara Leoni, the great erotic passion of the Roman years, he takes a hermitage above the trabocchi: the spider-legged fishing machines of the Chieti coast. The ginestra blazes on the cliff; the lovers live on bread, fruit and each other. Out of this summer he will build Il Trionfo della Morte, setting Giorgio Aurispa's final leap from these very rocks. The landscape is promoted to scripture: the Abruzzo coast enters European literature as a place where love and death share one house.
suggested_refs: Eremo dannunziano, San Vito Chietino; the trabocchi of the Costa dei Trabocchi

stops.name: Rome, the cavalry year with the Cavalleggeri di Alessandria
stops.campa: Called at last to military service, the aesthete astonishes everyone by excelling at it. A year with the Cavalleggeri di Alessandria: he rides superbly, endures gladly, and discovers in the barracks a taste that will outlast every drawing-room: the taste for soldiering. The officers find the famous poet the hardest man in the squadron to tire. Horse, saber, trumpet at dawn: the future Comandante is founded here, though for now he returns his commission and goes back to his debts and his novels.
suggested_refs: d'Annunzio in cavalry uniform, 1889-1890 photographs

segments.name: Napoli e i ritorni d'Abruzzo: the splendid misery

stops.name: Naples, arrival into the splendid misery
stops.campa: Fleeing Roman creditors in August 1891, he comes down to Naples for a fortnight and stays two years. He will call it his splendida miseria: pawned watches, borrowed dress-shirts, and meanwhile the richest prose of his life. Naples gives him Wagner in the salons, the Neapolitan press at his feet, and the Countess Maria Gravina di Ramacca, who abandons husband and children for him and is convicted of adultery beside him. He is poor as a saint and lives like a cardinal.
suggested_refs: Naples, Riviera di Chiaia in the 1890s

stops.name: Corriere di Napoli, L'Innocente in serial, the name crosses the Alps
stops.campa: In the pages of Scarfoglio and Serao's Corriere di Napoli, L'Innocente runs in serial through the winter: the Tolstoyan novel of a husband who lets his wife's bastard die of the cold. France reads it as L'Intrus and Europe learns the name d'Annunzio; Eleonora Duse reads it and writes to the author she has not yet met, asking him for a work worthy of her. The letter is an annunciation he files away. Giovanni Episcopo follows; the Russian masters have passed through him and come out Latin.
suggested_refs: Corriere di Napoli serialization of L'Innocente, 1891-1892

stops.name: Francavilla al Mare, Il Trionfo della Morte finished at the Conventino
stops.campa: Back under Michetti's roof, ruined and radiant, he completes Il Trionfo della Morte, the book of the Trabocchi coast and of Barbara, Ippolita in its pages, and dedicates it to Michetti himself. The novel closes the Romances of the Rose: desire studied until it becomes fatal. From Naples he has carried Nietzsche north in his baggage; the Superman enters Italian letters through an Abruzzo convent window. The province that made him now has its epic of blood, saints' shrines and the deaf pull of the sea.
suggested_refs: Trionfo della Morte first edition (Treves, 1894); Michetti's Le figlie di Iorio canvas

stops.name: Athens, the cruise of the Fantasia, Greece touched with the hands
stops.campa: In the summer of 1895 he sails the Aegean on Scarfoglio's yacht Fantasia with Georges Hérelle, his French translator, aboard. Patras, Olympia, Mycenae, Athens: he climbs the Acropolis in white flannel and takes possession of Hellas as a legacy owed to him. The companions record seasickness and brothels; he records the marble and the light. From this cruise the Laus Vitae of Maia will rise years later: eight thousand verses making the voyage into the myth of Ulysses renewed in an Italian body.
stops.quote: O Vita, o Vita, dono terribile del dio, come una spada fedele, come una ruggente face...
suggested_refs: The Acropolis of Athens; Maia (Laudi, book I)

stops.name: Venice, the Hotel Danieli, Eleonora Duse
stops.campa: On 26 September 1895, at the Hotel Danieli, the poet and Eleonora Duse are joined at last. She has read the Trionfo and calls him the infernal poet; after the first night she sends him a note of three words, Vedo il sole, I see the sun, and names the meeting a solar enchantment. The greatest actress alive and the poet who intends to be the greatest anything alive: for eight years Italian theatre will be their correspondence made flesh. The lagoon seals the pact.
suggested_refs: Hotel Danieli, Riva degli Schiavoni; portraits of Duse by Edward Gordon Craig circle

stops.name: Venice, L'Allegoria dell'Autunno in the Doge's Palace
stops.campa: In November 1895, for the city that has just invented its Biennale, he delivers L'Allegoria dell'Autunno: Venice preached to Venice, the dying season made a theory of art. The orator discovers his second instrument: not the page but the vaulted hall, the crowd breathing with the sentence. Out of this autumn will come Il Fuoco and its Stelio Effrena, the imaginary orator whose speeches the real one has already given. Venice is annexed to the legend; the legend will repay her with the Casetta Rossa and the Notturno.
suggested_refs: Palazzo Ducale, Sala del Maggior Consiglio; first Venice Biennale, 1895

stops.name: Pescara, the Discorso della siepe, the deputy of Beauty
stops.campa: In August 1897 he stands for parliament in the college of Ortona as the candidato della Bellezza, the candidate of Beauty, and at a banquet near Pescara delivers the Discorso della siepe, the Speech of the Hedge: property, land and the peasant's hedge sung as sacred forms. The Abruzzo, amused and proud, elects its poet. He enters Montecitorio announcing that he brings culture among the barbarians, and votes rarely, gloriously, and only for spectacle. Politics has been annexed to aesthetics; the rehearsal for Fiume begins here.
suggested_refs: Discorso della siepe text, August 1897; election of Ortona a Mare

segments.name: La Capponcina: the years of Duse and the ruin

stops.name: Settignano, La Capponcina taken, the court of the borzois
stops.campa: Above Florence, at Settignano, he installs himself in the villa La Capponcina and furnishes it like a Renaissance reliquary on credit: damasks, lecterns, casts of the Parthenon frieze, forty greyhounds and borzois, horses named out of Ariosto. Eleonora Duse takes the Porziuncola close by; the two houses signal to each other across the olive terraces. Here he writes standing at a monk's desk, dressed like a Quattrocento page. The creditors circle for twelve years before they are permitted to exist.
suggested_refs: Villa La Capponcina, via della Capponcina, Settignano; photographs of d'Annunzio with borzois

stops.name: La Capponcina, La Gioconda for the Duse of the beautiful hands
stops.campa: For Eleonora he writes La Gioconda, the tragedy of the sculptor between wife and muse, and sets on its threshold the most courtly dedication in the Italian theatre: to Eleonora Duse of the beautiful hands. In the play the wife's hands are crushed saving the rival's statue; Duse plays the mutilation nightly with her sleeves pinned empty. The public understands that the poet gives his lover masterpieces the way other men give rings, and that every gift is also a wound prepared in advance.
stops.quote: A Eleonora Duse dalle belle mani.
suggested_refs: La Gioconda first edition dedication page; Duse in La Gioconda

stops.name: Milan, Il Fuoco published, the love betrayed in print
stops.campa: In March 1900 Treves of Milan issues Il Fuoco, and Europe reads, barely veiled, the anatomy of his nights with Duse: Foscarina, the great actress aging, studied like a specimen by the young orator who loves and uses her. The scandal is continental; friends beg her to stop the book. She refuses: her suffering, she says, does not count when another masterpiece is to be given to Italian literature. It is the most complete sentence of love and the most complete betrayal in the canon, and both are true.
suggested_refs: Il Fuoco first edition (Treves, 1900)

stops.name: Rome, Montecitorio, the walk toward life
stops.campa: In the chamber, during the debates on the laws of public safety, the deputy of Beauty rises from the benches of the Right, crosses the floor before the whole parliament, and sits with the Extreme Left, saying that as a man of intellect he goes toward life. The gesture is pure theatre and pure omen: he belongs to no party but motion itself. In the next elections the seat is lost and never missed. Parliaments, he has learned, are rooms; he requires balconies.
stops.quote: Come uomo d'intelletto, vado verso la vita.
stops.quote_source: Declaration in the Chamber of Deputies, March 1900
suggested_refs: Palazzo Montecitorio; parliamentary chronicles, March 1900

stops.name: Rome, Teatro Costanzi, Francesca da Rimini with Duse
stops.campa: On 9 December 1901, at the Costanzi, Eleonora Duse is Francesca in the tragedy he has built for her out of Dante's fifth canto: a Malatesta Rimini reconstructed arch by arch, armourers' invoices and all, the most expensive staging Italy has seen. The poem of the kiss over the book, given back to the theatre six centuries later. The public quarrels, the box office triumphs, and the pair stand at the summit of their joined arts, exactly at the moment the descent is prepared.
suggested_refs: Teatro Costanzi (Teatro dell'Opera di Roma); Francesca da Rimini stage designs, 1901

stops.name: Marina di Pisa, the pine wood of the rain
stops.campa: The Alcyone summer: with Eleonora at Marina di Pisa, between the Arno mouth and the Tombolo pines, the Tuscan July and August of 1902 turn directly into verse. Rain comes over the pineta and the two lovers walking in it are changed into vegetable creatures, faces dripping green: La pioggia nel pineto is written as weather. Ermione walks here forever. The greatest Italian lyric sequence of the century is a holiday diary; the canon holds that for one season a man transcribed the Mediterranean itself.
stops.quote: Taci. Su le soglie del bosco non odo parole che dici umane; ma odo parole più nuove che parlano gocciole e foglie lontane.
suggested_refs: Pineta di Marina di Pisa (Tombolo); Alcyone first edition

stops.name: Milan, Teatro Lirico, La figlia di Iorio without Duse
stops.campa: On 2 March 1904 the Teatro Lirico gives La figlia di Iorio, the pastoral tragedy of the Abruzzo: Mila di Codra hunted by reapers, the ancient shepherd world made liturgy. It is his greatest theatrical triumph, and Eleonora Duse is not on the stage: ill at Genoa, she is replaced by Irma Gramatica, and the role written in her blood is given away. The wound is final. The love of the age ends not with a scene but with a casting decision; Duse and the poet do not meet again for twenty years.
suggested_refs: La figlia di Iorio premiere playbill, Teatro Lirico 1904; Michetti's La figlia di Iorio (1895)

stops.name: Montichiari, the Brescia air circuit, the poet takes wing
stops.campa: At the Brescia air meeting of September 1909, on the plain of Montichiari, he climbs behind Glenn Curtiss and leaves the earth for the first time. Kafka is in the crowd, taking notes on the small stern-faced Italian celebrity. The flight lasts minutes; the conversion lasts the rest of his life. Icarus enters the Laudi; the novel Forse che sì forse che no gives Italy its first aviator hero. He has found the machine adequate to his myth, and he already knows there is a war coming that will require it.
suggested_refs: Circuito aereo di Brescia 1909; Kafka's Die Aeroplane in Brescia

stops.name: Settignano, the creditors take the Capponcina
stops.campa: The arithmetic arrives at last. In March 1910, hounded by a mountain of protested bills, he leaves the Capponcina by night: the greyhounds, the casts, the damasks, the four thousand books all abandoned to the bailiffs, who will auction the whole reliquary piece by piece the following year. He does not watch. Ruin is reframed as departure: the ship for France is called exile, and exile is called a Latin poet's right. The villa empties; the legend, unencumbered, travels light.
suggested_refs: Auction catalogue of the Capponcina seizures, 1911

stops.name: Paris, the exile arrives and is crowned
stops.campa: Paris receives the fugitive as a reigning prince of letters: Montesquiou presents him, the salons dispute him, Ida Rubinstein and the Ballets Russes orbit near. He arrives owing everything and within a month is dining as the guest of honour of the Republic of taste. He writes now in French as well, to the scandal and admiration of the Académie's antechambers. The exile is golden by his own decree: Italy, he lets it be known, is not lost but merely waiting for him to be necessary.
suggested_refs: Boldini and La Gandara portraits of the Paris years

stops.name: Arcachon, the Villa Saint-Dominique among the dunes
stops.campa: At Le Moulleau by Arcachon he takes the Villa Saint-Dominique, pines and ocean and the great dune southward: an Atlantic Landes to replace the lost Tuscan hill. Greyhounds again, horses again, debts again, and the work pouring out: French dramas, the martyrology, the odes. Nathalie de Goloubeff, the amazon of the kennels, keeps his hounds and his heart's ledger. He rides the empty beaches in winter and calls the fog of Gascony a good workshop for an Italian who is preparing thunder.
suggested_refs: Villa Saint-Dominique, Le Moulleau; photographs with the Goloubeff greyhounds

stops.name: Paris, Théâtre du Châtelet, Le Martyre de Saint Sébastien
stops.campa: On 22 May 1911 the Châtelet gives Le Martyre de Saint Sébastien: his French verse mystery, Debussy's music, Bakst's décor, Ida Rubinstein's androgynous saint pierced by arrows. A week before the opening the Archbishop of Paris forbids Catholics to attend, and Rome places the poet's works on the Index: the martyrdom is thus performed twice, once on stage and once upon the author, exactly as he would have written it. Debussy and the Jew Rubinstein and the pagan d'Annunzio, censured together, take their bows.
suggested_refs: Bakst's designs for Le Martyre de Saint Sébastien; Debussy's score

stops.name: Arcachon, the Canzoni della gesta d'oltremare
stops.campa: When Italy goes to Libya, the exile's desk becomes a battery. From Arcachon he fires the Canzoni della gesta d'oltremare into the Corriere della Sera: the songs of the overseas deed, Dante's metres retooled for dreadnoughts and desert columns. One canzone insults Austria so directly that the censor blanks it out, and the blank page is read more avidly than any verses. From the Atlantic dunes he has resumed command of Italian patriotism by post. The nation notices that its war poet lives abroad, and is ashamed.
suggested_refs: Merope (Canzoni delle gesta d'oltremare), 1912; the censored Canzone dei Dardanelli

stops.name: Paris, the summons: Quarto calls the exile home
stops.campa: Spring 1915: Italy hangs between neutrality and the war, and the letter comes to Paris: the invitation to speak at Quarto, where Garibaldi's Thousand embarked, at the unveiling of their monument. He recognizes the shape of the hour instantly: a nation requiring a voice, a shore requiring a prophet, five years of exile requiring an ending. He drafts the oration in the French capital while the French armies hold the Marne. The debts remain in France; the man is repatriated by destiny, first class.
suggested_refs: Invitation correspondence for the Quarto inauguration, April 1915

segments.name: Il maggio radioso e la guerra del poeta, 1915-1918

stops.name: Genoa, the landing of the exile
stops.campa: On 4 May 1915 he crosses the frontier and comes down to Genoa, and the crowds are already at the stations as if a sovereign travelled. Five years of exile end in flowers and delirium. The government that half-invited him is already frightened of him; the neutralist parliament holds the majority, but the piazzas from this hour belong to the poet. He sleeps little, corrects the speech, and looks out at the harbour from which the Thousand sailed. Tomorrow he will talk a kingdom into a war.
suggested_refs: Genoa, May 1915 press photographs of the arrival

stops.name: Quarto dei Mille, the Sagra dei Mille, the speech from the rock
stops.campa: On 5 May 1915, before the bronze of Garibaldi's Thousand and a sea of twenty thousand, he preaches the new Sermon on the Mount: the beatitudes rewritten for a nation hungry for war. Blessed are the young, hungry and thirsty for glory, for they shall be satisfied. The King has stayed away; the government trembles at every clause. From the rock of Quarto the interventionist May is ignited, the radiant May, and Italy is talked toward the trenches by a poet, an event without precedent in the modern chronicles.
stops.quote: Beati i giovani che sono affamati e assetati di gloria, perché saranno saziati... O beati quelli che più hanno, perché più potranno dare, più potranno ardere.
suggested_refs: Monumento ai Mille, Quarto; Discorso di Quarto full text

stops.name: Rome, the balcony of the Hotel Regina
stops.campa: In Rome the radiant May boils. From the balcony of the Hotel Regina on Via Veneto he harangues the crowds night after night, naming the neutralist Giolitti a traitor, calling for the parliament of the old Italy to be swept into the Tiber. The city answers with torchlight processions. Ministers consider arresting him and discover it is no longer possible: the crowd has become an organ of his voice. The technique of the balcony, the sacred dialogue of Comandante and piazza, is founded here, and others are watching who will use it for twenty years.
suggested_refs: Hotel Regina, Via Veneto; chronicles of the maggio radioso

stops.name: Rome, the Campidoglio oration
stops.campa: On the Capitoline, navel of the Latin world, he gives the last and greatest of the May orations, unsheathing the sword of Nino Bixio before the crowd. Rome above him, Rome beneath him: he speaks as if the she-wolf herself had retained counsel. Within the week the Chamber capitulates, full powers are voted, and on 24 May Italy enters the war. The poet has his war; the war, though it does not know it yet, has its poet: fifty-two years old, half-blind with ambition, demanding a uniform.
suggested_refs: Campidoglio, 17 May 1915; Per la più grande Italia (collected orations)

stops.name: Over Trieste, the first flight of the poet-aviator
stops.campa: On 7 August 1915, lieutenant of the Novara Lancers seconded to the air, he flies with Giuseppe Miraglia over unredeemed Trieste and lets fall not bombs but messages weighted with ribbons: courage, brothers, the end of your patience is near. The Austrians answer with anti-aircraft fire; he notes the black flowers of the bursts with a connoisseur's calm. The war of the poet-aviator begins: every mission a canto, every city a stanza to be liberated. Miraglia, the beloved pilot, has four months to live.
suggested_refs: Trieste under Austria, 1915; d'Annunzio and Miraglia photographs

stops.name: Grado, the forced landing, the eye given to the war
stops.campa: On 16 January 1916 the seaplane returning from Grado strikes the water hard and the poet's temple strikes the machine-gun butt. He flies again within days, hiding the wound; when the doctors finally look, the right eye is lost, the retina detached, the left threatened. The omen is read aloud by destiny: the seer half-blinded, like every seer of the old stories, at the exact price of second sight. He accepts the tariff without bargaining and asks how soon a one-eyed man may fly.
suggested_refs: Grado lagoon; the bandaged d'Annunzio portraits, 1916

stops.name: Venice, the dark room of the Casetta Rossa, Notturno on paper strips
stops.campa: In the little red house on the Grand Canal he lies bandaged in the dark, head lower than his feet, forbidden to move, forbidden light. His daughter Renata, Sirenetta, cuts ten thousand strips of paper, one line wide, and on these cartigli, blind, he writes the Notturno: the sounds of Venice at war coming across the water, the dead pilots visiting the dark room, memory operating like sonar. The prose of a sightless man becomes the newest in Italian. Even mutilation, the canon observes, he converts into an instrument.
stops.quote: Ho gli occhi bendati. Sto supino nel letto, col torso immobile, col capo riverso... Scrivo sopra una stretta lista di carta che contiene una riga.
suggested_refs: Casetta Rossa, Grand Canal; the cartigli of the Notturno (Vittoriale archives)

stops.name: The mouth of the Timavo, Randaccio's flag
stops.campa: With the infantry now, he carries a tricolour meant to be raised over Duino and marches with Major Giovanni Randaccio on the night attack at the Timavo: the river of the Argonauts, the river with the underground course, the most mythological water on the front. The attack breaks; Randaccio takes his death-wound and dies with the flag for a pillow. The poet brings the bloodied banner back and will sleep beneath it at the Vittoriale for twenty years. The Timavo enters his personal liturgy: where the river goes under the rock, the friend went under the earth.
suggested_refs: The Randaccio flag (Vittoriale, Stanza delle Reliquie); mouths of the Timavo at San Giovanni di Duino

stops.name: Over Cattaro, the long night raid
stops.campa: In the night of 4-5 October 1917 he rides a bomber of the San Marco squadron across the whole Adriatic to the Bocche di Cattaro, the deep fjord where the Austrian fleet sleeps behind its mountains. Hours over open sea, engines against the bora, the bombs laid into the anchorage, and the return at dawn. He is fifty-four years old and the youngest man on the raid by his own account. The Adriatic, he repeats, is a gulf and the gulf is Italian: the war of the poet is a cartography lesson delivered by air.
suggested_refs: Bocche di Cattaro (Boka Kotorska); San Marco squadron records

stops.name: Bakar, the Beffa di Buccari, thirty of one fate
stops.campa: In the night of 10-11 February 1918 three tiny MAS torpedo boats slip forty miles up the enemy's own gulf into the bay of Buccari and loose their torpedoes among the anchored shipping. The material damage is nothing; the wound to Austrian pride is immense. Before withdrawing, the poet sets three sealed bottles afloat, dressed in tricolour ribbons, each carrying his mockery in ink. Out of the raid comes the song, thirty of one fate, and thirty-one with death, and the motto he coins for the MAS: Memento audere semper.
stops.quote: In onta alla cautissima Flotta austriaca... sono venuti col ferro e col fuoco a scuotere la prudenza nel suo più comodo rifugio i marinai d'Italia, che si ridono d'ogni sorta di reti e di sbarre, pronti sempre a osare l'inosabile.
stops.quote_source: Message sealed in the bottles of Buccari, 10-11 February 1918
suggested_refs: MAS 96 (preserved at the Vittoriale); La Canzone del Quarnaro

stops.name: San Pelagio, dawn of the Vienna flight
stops.campa: At 5:50 in the morning of 9 August 1918, from the field of San Pelagio near Padua, eleven SVA biplanes of the 87th Squadriglia La Serenissima lift off for Vienna: a thousand kilometres over the Alps, at the extreme edge of fuel and possibility. The poet rides in the modified two-seater, fifty-five years old, one-eyed, forbidden the mission by every authority and obeyed by none of them. Seven machines will hold the course. On the fuselages, the lion of Saint Mark; in the lockers, fifty thousand leaflets in his hand and three hundred fifty thousand in Ojetti's plainer prose.
suggested_refs: Castello di San Pelagio (Museo dell'Aria); the SVA of the raid (Vittoriale)

stops.name: Vienna, the leaflets over the enemy capital
stops.campa: At 9:20 the tricolour wing appears over Vienna. No bombs: paper. The leaflets spiral down onto the Graben and the Stephansplatz: we could be dropping tonnes of explosive, they say; we drop instead a three-coloured greeting, the three colours of liberty. Viennese crowds look up at the impossible Italians strolling the sky of the Habsburg capital. Not a shot rises. The squadron turns home with empty racks and full glory, and the war of the poet reaches the form it was always seeking: an air raid composed entirely of rhetoric.
stops.quote: In questo mattino d'agosto, mentre si compie il quarto anno della vostra convulsione disperata e luminosamente incomincia l'anno della nostra piena energia... VIENNESI!
stops.quote_source: D'Annunzio's autograph leaflet dropped over Vienna, 9 August 1918
suggested_refs: The Vienna leaflets (both texts); route map of the Volo su Vienna

stops.name: Venice, victory, and the word 'mutilated'
stops.campa: As the last offensive opens on the Piave, he publishes in the Corriere della Sera the letter to the dead: our Victory, you shall not be mutilated. The phrase outlives the war it was written to bless. When the armistice comes and the diplomats at Paris begin trimming the Adriatic promises, vittoria mutilata is already minted, waiting in every mouth. The poet has done the most dangerous of his deeds: he has given a grievance its name. Names, in his hands, mobilize like divisions.
suggested_refs: Corriere della Sera, 24 October 1918; Paris Peace Conference Adriatic question

segments.name: Fiume o morte: la Città olocausta, 1919-1921

stops.name: Ronchi, the night muster of the granatieri
stops.campa: In the night of 11-12 September 1919, at Ronchi where the grenadiers expelled from Fiume wait in their billets, the Comandante arrives by motorcar, feverish, to lead the march the government has forbidden. Some two hundred men and a column of commandeered trucks: the marcia di Ronchi. He tells them the die is cast and better than Caesar's, for they cross not a river but a sentence of the diplomats. The village will take the name Ronchi dei Legionari from this night, the calendar of the myth beginning at its gate.
suggested_refs: Ronchi dei Legionari; the oath of Ronchi in legionary memoirs

stops.name: Cantrida, the roadblock, the breast of medals
stops.campa: At Cantrida, on the western approach to Fiume, General Pittaluga's armoured cars bar the road with orders to stop the column at any cost. The Comandante descends, opens his greatcoat over the gold medal and the ribbons of the war, and offers the general his chest: fire on these first. The soldiers sent to stop him present arms instead; the armoured cars swing round and join the column. The canon records the moment as the modern miracle of the loaves: an army fed to the rebellion by the act of refusing to shoot it.
stops.quote_source: To General Pittaluga at Cantrida, 12 September 1919 (as recorded in the Fiume chronicles and Pittaluga's memoirs)
suggested_refs: Kantrida, Rijeka; accounts of the Pittaluga confrontation

stops.name: Fiume, the Santa Entrata
stops.campa: Toward noon of 12 September 1919 the column enters Fiume through streets gone mad with flowers and flags sewn in secret. Women weep on the running-boards; the bells of the Italian churches ring themselves hoarse. The city that the Peace Conference has assigned to no one receives its Comandante as a bridegroom: the tradition names the day the Santa Entrata, the Holy Entry, and means the Gospel echo. A poet has taken a city with two hundred men and a fever, and not one shot has been required of history.
suggested_refs: Corso of Fiume, 12 September 1919 photographs; the Santa Entrata in legionary iconography

stops.name: Fiume, the balcony of the Governor's Palace, the proclamation
stops.campa: At six in the evening, still burning with fever, he steps onto the balcony of the Governor's Palace above a piazza packed to the walls. In the mad and vile world, he tells them, Fiume is today the sign of liberty; there is one truth, and it is Fiume; one love, and it is Fiume. He proclaims the annexation to Italy in the name of the sound people of the nation and asks the crowd to confirm its vote before the flag of the Timavo: the Randaccio banner spread on the parapet. The piazza thunders yes three times. The Comandante governs from this balcony for fifteen months.
stops.quote: Italiani di Fiume! Nel mondo folle e vile, Fiume oggi è il segno della libertà; nel mondo folle e vile vi è una sola cosa pura: Fiume; vi è una sola verità: e questa è Fiume; vi è un solo amore: e questo è Fiume!
stops.quote_source: Proclamation from the Governor's Palace balcony, 12 September 1919
suggested_refs: Governor's Palace, Rijeka; balcony speech photographs and film

stops.name: Fiume, the modus vivendi refused, Hic manebimus optime
stops.campa: In December Rome offers the compromise: the modus vivendi, an Italian protectorate in ordinary prose. The city's council inclines to accept; the plebiscite of 18 December votes for it; and the Comandante, reading in the urns a will unworthy of the dead, annuls the count and answers with the old Roman word: here we shall remain, excellently. Fiume passes from adventure to heresy: a city-state run on orations, piracy and festival, where deserters arrive weekly and the futurists, the syndicalists and the uscocchi of the new age gather as at a court of miracles.
stops.quote_source: Motto adopted by d'Annunzio at Fiume, December 1919
suggested_refs: The modus vivendi documents; Fiume legionary life photographs, 1920

stops.name: Fiume, the Carta del Carnaro, music made a fundamental institution
stops.campa: On 8 September 1920 he proclaims the Reggenza Italiana del Carnaro and gives it the constitution drafted with Alceste De Ambris and rewritten in his own tongue: the Carta del Carnaro. Corporations and communes, equality of women, freedom of every cult; and, alone among the constitutions of the earth, music enthroned as a religious and social institution of the state, with choirs and instruments decreed for every commune and an auditorium of ten thousand souls. The lawgiver-poet completes the arc begun at Quarto: the state itself composed as a lyric.
stops.quote: Nella Reggenza italiana del Carnaro la Musica è una istituzione religiosa e sociale.
stops.quote_source: Carta del Carnaro, article LXIV (Della Musica), 8 September 1920
suggested_refs: Carta del Carnaro printed text; Reggenza Italiana del Carnaro flag with the Ursa Major and the ouroboros

stops.name: Fiume, the Natale di sangue, the Christmas of Blood
stops.campa: The Treaty of Rapallo makes Fiume a free state and the Comandante refuses the gift as an amputation. At Christmas 1920 the regular army and navy of Italy move against the city of Italians: the Natale di sangue. On 26 December the battleship Andrea Doria puts a shell into the Governor's Palace itself, the splinters falling in the Comandante's rooms. Legionaries die under Italian guns at Italian walls. He had sworn Fiume o morte; confronting instead this fratricide, he declares that Italy is not worth the dying of her best sons, and the myth chooses survival: to build its shrine elsewhere.
suggested_refs: Damage to the Governor's Palace, December 1920; Natale di sangue chronicles

stops.name: Fiume, the farewell of the Comandante
stops.campa: On 18 January 1921, the powers signed away and the dead buried, the Comandante leaves Fiume by motorcar as quietly as he entered it loudly. The city lines the streets in silence; many of the legionaries weep, and some will wander for years like soldiers of a disbanded crusade. He carries away the flag of Randaccio, the ashes of his dead, and the working model of every theatrical seizure of power the century will stage. Behind him the holocaust city, la Città olocausta, the city offered whole, enters the martyrology he wrote for it.
suggested_refs: Departure photographs, January 1921; legionary diaspora memoirs

stops.name: Gardone Riviera, Villa Cargnacco taken above the lake
stops.campa: In February 1921 he rents, then possesses, the villa of Cargnacco on the hill over Gardone Riviera: a sequestered German scholar's house with a library and a view of the whole of Garda. The same water Goethe rowed under the cliffs of Malcesine glitters below; the lake of the northern pilgrims becomes the lake of the last condottiere. He announces a retreat and begins, immediately, a construction: not a house but a self, built in stone, to be called the Vittoriale degli Italiani: the shrine of Italian victories, of which he is the chief exhibit.
suggested_refs: Villa Cargnacco (the Prioria); Lake Garda from the Vittoriale terraces

stops.name: The Vittoriale, the fall from the window, the flight of the archangel
stops.campa: On the night of 13 August 1922, on the eve of a meeting with Mussolini and Nitti that might have set him at the head of the national movement, the Comandante falls from a window of the Prioria and fractures his skull. Pushed, jumped, or slipped beside the sister of his mistress; the canon leaves the agent unnamed and calls the event il volo dell'arcangelo, the archangel's flight. He lies between death and life while the March on Rome is prepared by other men. When he wakes, the century has been assigned to Mussolini, and the poet has been assigned to the lake.
suggested_refs: The Prioria windows; press of August 1922 on the incidente

stops.name: The Vittoriale, the March on Rome passes by in silence
stops.campa: October 1922: the blackshirts march on Rome using his choreography, the oaths, the songs, the Roman salute, the balcony, all inventoried at Fiume, and the inventor keeps to his hill, convalescent and unconsulted. He neither blesses nor curses; his silence is read in Rome twice a day like a barometer. The regime will pay for that silence lavishly for sixteen years: editions of his works at state expense, the Vittoriale funded, honours heaped: the gilded muzzle. He accepts the gold and, in letters, occasionally bites.
suggested_refs: March on Rome newsreels; d'Annunzio-Mussolini correspondence

stops.name: The Vittoriale, the gift of the shrine to the Italian people
stops.campa: By deed of December 1923 he donates the Vittoriale, and himself with it, to the Italian people: the house, the relics, the manuscripts, the future mausoleum, all made national while the donor still lives in it, editing his own reliquary. Over the entrance he sets the motto of the whole economy of his life: I have what I have given. The state accepts, and thereby ratifies the doctrine: that the nation is the heir, and the poet's biography is public property, a gospel in objects.
stops.quote: Io ho quel che ho donato.
stops.quote_source: Motto inscribed at the entrance of the Vittoriale
suggested_refs: The Vittoriale entrance arch with the motto; deed of donation, 1923

stops.name: The Vittoriale, Principe di Montenevoso
stops.campa: When Fiume is at last annexed to Italy in 1924, the King raises the poet to the rank of prince: Principe di Montenevoso, prince of the Snowy Mountain, the peak that marks the new eastern border. The title is a treaty written as heraldry: the state paying its debt to the man who made the border imaginable. He, who began as the notary's grandson of Pescara and styled himself duke in a newspaper, ends in the almanac of the nobility by act of parliament, ennobled for a city he took against the government's orders.
suggested_refs: Royal decree of March 1924; Monte Nevoso (Snežnik)

stops.name: The Vittoriale, Mussolini comes as a pilgrim
stops.campa: The Duce comes up the hill to the poet, not the poet down to Rome. Mussolini is received among the relics, shown the flag of Randaccio, and conducted through rooms arranged like the stations of a private religion. The two seducers of crowds measure each other with perfect courtesy and perfect mistrust. Mussolini departs having paid for everything and secured one thing: that the archangel will thunder only from his own hill. The canon keeps the visit as the meeting of the church and the state of the Italian myth, and leaves delicately unsaid which was which.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Mussolini at the Vittoriale; the Stanza delle Reliquie

stops.name: The Vittoriale, the prow of the Puglia set in the hillside
stops.campa: The Navy gives him the cruiser Puglia, the ship of the Adriatic vigils, whose captain was killed at Split, and he has her bow carried up the hill in pieces and rebuilt jutting from the cypresses, prow aimed across Garda toward the Adriatic she can no longer reach. A warship run aground in a garden, crewed by memory: no emblem of the mutilated victory could be more literal, and none more serene. Above her he hangs the SVA of Vienna in the auditorium, and moors the MAS of Buccari below: the whole war, dry-docked in paradise.
suggested_refs: The Nave Puglia in the Vittoriale gardens; the SVA of the Vienna flight in the Auditorium; MAS 96

stops.name: The Vittoriale, Il libro segreto, the last mask
stops.campa: Old now, sleepless on cocaine and memory, he publishes under the mask of Angelo Cocles the Cento e cento e cento e cento pagine del libro segreto: the hundred and hundred and hundred and hundred pages of the secret book of Gabriele d'Annunzio tempted to die. The prose breaks into fragments, confession, and night-thoughts: the inventor of the inimitable life files its final inventory. The dandy, the Comandante, the prince recede; what remains at the desk is a lucid, half-blind old craftsman of Italian, testing whether the language can still lift.
suggested_refs: Il libro segreto (1935), first edition

stops.name: Verona, the station, the last warning to Mussolini
stops.campa: September 1937: Mussolini returns by rail from the German triumph, and the old poet comes down from his hill to meet the train at Verona. On the platform, the last encounter: d'Annunzio urges him against binding Italy to Hitler, the Germany he has long mocked in his letters, and pleads the old Latin sea against the new northern axis. The Duce embraces him, promises nothing, and steams south. It is the final public act of the Comandante: a prophecy delivered in a railway station, unheeded, and, the canon notes, exact.
suggested_refs: Verona Porta Nuova station; d'Annunzio's anti-German letters to Mussolini (1933-1937)

stops.name: The Vittoriale, death at the writing desk in the Zambracca
stops.campa: On 1 March 1938, at 8:05 in the evening, seated at the little desk of the Zambracca where he answered letters and kept his medicines, the poet's head drops to the wood: cerebral hemorrhage, instant. He dies writing: the one death, of all the deaths he drafted for himself since the horse on the road to Francavilla, that needed no press release. The lake is dark under the window. Mussolini orders state mourning; the telegrams call him the John the Baptist of the regime, and the family knows he would have corrected the theology and kept the capital letters.
suggested_refs: The Zambracca room, Prioria; Istituto Luce newsreel of the death announcement

stops.name: The mausoleum above the lake, the Comandante among his legionaries
stops.campa: They bury him on the hill with a state funeral, and later raise over him the mausoleum he had planned: three concentric rings of stone on the highest terrace, the tombs of ten legionaries of Fiume in a circle and the Comandante lifted at the centre, above the cypresses, above the Puglia's prow, above the water. From the summit the whole of Garda lies open to the south: Goethe's lake and his, the German pilgrim's road and the Italian archangel's roost, one water. The journey that began on a river-port in the Abruzzo ends in white stone in the air: the life, as promised, inimitable.
suggested_refs: The Mausoleum of the Vittoriale; the legionary tombs; Lake Garda panorama
